performers: Marine Chamber Orchestra of the United States Marine Band; Maj. Jason K. Fettig, conductor
intro: The Air, marked Andante religioso, is the slow G minor fourth movement of Grieg’s From Holberg’s Time, Op. 40, for strings, written in honour of a playwright born in Bergen in 1684. The Marine Chamber Orchestra plays it under Jason K. Fettig.

B · Middle section in B♭ major
A′ · The melody comes back
sections.mNote: G minor again, with the lower strings in the tune.

sections.label: Coda · Fading to a held chord

cues.title: Air, G minor
cues.text: Andante religioso, G minor, in 3/4, marked cantabile. The upper and lower strings share the melody. Suspensions run through the harmony, with notes held against the chord and then resolved.
cues.evidence: Grieg, Holberg Suite Op. 40, Air: G minor, 3/4, Andante religioso ♩ = 54, cantabile, in the piano version (bars 68–82 of the typeset edition on IMSLP, PMLP08562): https://archive.org/details/imslp-suite-op40-grieg-edvard. Matthew Mendez, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note: sighing melodic figures, poignant suspensions, upper and lower strings sharing the main melody: https://www.bso.org/works/grieg-holberg-suite
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repeat of the opening strain
cues.text: The opening strain is played a second time, as its repeat sign directs, with its crescendo and diminuendo.
cues.evidence: Grieg, Holberg Suite, Air, piano version: repeat sign at the end of the opening strain, bar 82 (typeset edition on IMSLP, PMLP08562): https://archive.org/details/imslp-suite-op40-grieg-edvard
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Middle section in B♭ major
cues.text: The middle section moves to B♭ major, the relative major. Here Grieg uses the full sonority of the Romantic string orchestra, and the music builds steadily.
cues.evidence: Matthew Mendez, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note: “a middle section in the relative major makes full use of the richer sonorities afforded by Romantic-era string forces”: https://www.bso.org/works/grieg-holberg-suite
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Holberg bicentenary, 1884
cues.text: Grieg called From Holberg’s Time “a good exercise for concealing one’s own personality”. He wrote it for the 200th anniversary of Ludvig Holberg’s birth, on 3 December 1884, first as a piano suite and then, in 1885, for strings.
cues.evidence: Matthew Mendez, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note: Grieg’s description of the suite as “a good exercise for concealing one’s own personality”; piano version for the bicentenary celebrations, string version completed by March 1885: https://www.bso.org/works/grieg-holberg-suite. Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon: occasion was the 200th anniversary of Holberg’s birth, 3 December 1884: https://nbl.snl.no/Edvard_Grieg

cues.title: Return of the opening melody
cues.text: The opening melody returns in G minor, shared between the upper and lower strings. The music builds to a climax near the end; in Grieg’s piano version the melody returns in the left hand at bar 107 and builds to ffz at bar 121.
cues.evidence: Grieg, Holberg Suite, Air, piano version: the “mf cantabile” melody returns in the left hand at bar 107, building to ffz at bar 121 (typeset edition on IMSLP, PMLP08562): https://archive.org/details/imslp-suite-op40-grieg-edvard. Matthew Mendez, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note: both upper and lower strings take part in the main melody: https://www.bso.org/works/grieg-holberg-suite
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars
cues.text: After the last climax the tempo slows and the texture thins, with dim. and ritardando leading down to pp. The final chord is held under a pause.
cues.evidence: Grieg, Holberg Suite, Air, piano version, bars 121–123: ffz, “dim e ritardando”, “più ritard.”, fp to pp, and a fermata (typeset edition on IMSLP, PMLP08562): https://archive.org/details/imslp-suite-op40-grieg-edvard
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer, the son of a Bergen merchant, who used Norwegian fiddle tunes, a troll king and a wedding party in concert-hall music.
facts: Conductor in Christiania, 1866–74 · Harmonien, Bergen, 1880–82 · a state composer’s stipend from 1874
Rikard Nordraak 1864–65 · Piano Concerto 1869 · Peer Gynt 1876 · Troldhaugen 1885
Ten books of Lyric Pieces, about 170 songs, a piano concerto, stage music, a string quartet and five sonatas

quote.text: The most important thing is truth, the truth of feeling.
quote.source: Grieg to Julius Röntgen, May 1904, quoted in Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon

composer.background:
Edvard Grieg was born on 15 June 1843 in the family house at Strandgaten 152, above Bergen’s harbour. His father, Alexander, was a merchant and the British vice-consul; his mother, Gesine, who had studied singing, piano and theory in Hamburg, taught him the piano from the age of six. He hated scales. In his essay Min første Succes he recalled the day at five when he stretched up to the keyboard and found a third, a triad, a four-note chord and at last, with both hands, the five notes of a ninth. “That was a success!” he wrote. “Nothing since has been able to intoxicate me like this.”

In the summer of 1858 the violinist Ole Bull called without warning at the Griegs’ summer house at Landås. Edvard was made to play. Bull grew serious, talked quietly with the parents, then shook the boy in his own way and said: “You are going to Leipzig to become an artist!” On 6 October Grieg entered the Conservatory. He later called it “that damned Leipzig conservatory”, but he went free to the Gewandhaus rehearsals, saw Tannhäuser fourteen times, and heard Clara Schumann play her husband’s concerto. In the spring of 1860 tuberculosis ruined one of his lungs. That autumn, against the doctor’s advice, he went back.
